errors.english: Cognition that follows direct perception as a mere essence devoid of that is conceived as the generator of its own subjective aspect.
errors.why: The cognition following perception is the one that conceives (the mere nature devoid of that) as the producer of its own image; the English makes the cognition the thing conceived.

note: A sound rendering of a difficult Pramāṇa commentary on dream and waking cognition; one clause near the end has its subject and object confused.

errors.english: the thirteen (sanghadisesa) rules
errors.why: This is the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, so the Sanskrit saṅghāvaśeṣa is meant, not the Pali saṅghādisesa (the same applies to the second occurrence).

errors.english: and think to himself: Afterwards, I shall properly restore my downfalls according to the Dharma. This mental resolve is the blessing.
errors.why: In Vinaya, sems kyis byin gyis brlab pa means to make a mental determination (adhiṣṭhāna); there is no 'blessing', and the sentence says he should resolve in mind that he will remedy the offence afterwards.

fix.find: and think to himself: Afterwards, I shall properly restore my downfalls according to the Dharma. This mental resolve is the blessing.
fix.replace: and mentally resolve: Afterwards, I shall properly remedy my offences according to the Dharma.

errors.english: (uposatha)
errors.why: Uposatha is the Pali form; this Mūlasarvāstivāda text calls for the Sanskrit poṣadha/upoṣadha.

note: An accurate account of the five modes of Prātimokṣa recitation and the reciter's and elder's duties, marred by Pali term forms and a misreading of the mental-resolve formula as a 'blessing'.

errors.english: accumulating unique blame known to the wise
errors.why: The point is that the misdeed is unshared (borne by the doer alone, as the buffalo and butcher's-son examples go on to show); 'known to the wise' is not in the Tibetan.

errors.english: acting like a spiritual teacher or a lord
errors.why: The king should not slight others but treat them as he would his elders or a lord; he is not told to act like a teacher or lord himself.

note: A good translation of Candrakīrti's commentary on the king's pride and the butcher's son story; two phrases blur the argument.
A faithful rendering of the Sadāprarudita excerpt quoted in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, including its abbreviation markers.

errors.english: could the presently master-mind be the self? [note: literally: "the mind that has arisen"]
errors.why: da ltar byung ba'i sems is simply 'the present mind'; 'master-mind' is a garble and the note is beside the point.

fix.find: could the presently master-mind be the self? [note: literally: "the mind that has arisen"]
fix.replace: could the present mind be the self?

errors.english: how could the mind that is to be observed be observed?
errors.why: gang gis marks the mind by which observation would happen (the observing mind), not the mind that is observed.

note: The argument against identifying the self with past, future or present mind and the plantain simile are rendered well apart from one garbled phrase.

errors.english: Since it is possible for a cause to exist without the result, this also thoroughly expresses the answer to the claim that "non-perception does not prove the absence of the object."
errors.why: The whole quoted clause, including 'since a cause can exist without its effect', is the opponent's objection being answered; the English makes that premise the author's own.

fix.find: Since it is possible for a cause to exist without the result, this also thoroughly expresses the answer to the claim that "non-perception does not prove the absence of the object."
fix.replace: This also states the answer to the objection: "Since a cause can exist without its result, non-perception does not prove the absence of the object."

errors.english: Their reversal is the non-existence of non-perception. Because of that, even the perception is said to be non-existent.
errors.why: The absence of cognition and object is the non-existence established by (consisting in) non-perception, which is why it is called 'absence of perception'; 'non-existence of non-perception' inverts the sense.

note: The commentary on non-perception (anupalabdhi) is followed in outline, but the objection and reply are confused in one place and the key definition of the absence is garbled.

errors.english: This means that when we later explain the destruction of a pot and so forth, it is said that "that very thing does not arise," but nothing is actually established therein.
errors.why: 'chad par 'gyur ba here means 'is cut off' (the continuum of the pot ceases), not 'we will explain'; the point is that cessation only negates the arising of the next similar moment and affirms nothing.

fix.find: This means that when we later explain the destruction of a pot and so forth, it is said that "that very thing does not arise," but nothing is actually established therein.
fix.replace: This means that when a pot and so forth is cut off, the sense is only that "that very thing does not arise"; nothing at all is affirmed of it.

errors.english: # Whatever the nature of destruction is
errors.why: The cited verse line (begun on the previous side) is 'since [destruction] whose nature is the cutting-off of the continuum…'; it is made into a heading and the 'cutting-off of the continuum' is lost.

errors.english: An example of this is the relationship of smoke to fire.
errors.why: The example is fire in relation to smoke: fire causes smoke but not its diminution.

note: A clear rendering of the two kinds of destruction and the types of contradiction, with one misread verb and a quoted verse turned into a heading.

errors.english: The term "nest" refers to unread syllable
errors.why: The Tibetan simply begins the gloss ('"nest" means…'), which continues on the next side; 'unread syllable' is an artefact.

errors.english: By the non-pacification of you and the cowherd, it will become known
errors.why: ma here is most likely 'mother' and Zhi ba a personal name (the cowherd's mother Śāntā, whose hand throws the pot in the gloss), not a negation 'non-pacification' and 'the peaceful one'.

errors.english: milk-churner
errors.why: zho rdzi'u is a small pot of curd, not a churner.

note: Most of the word-glosses of this Vinaya commentary are rendered accurately; one gloss misreads a name, and a stray placeholder closes the page.

errors.english: the body of those with blind minds is thinned day by day by limbs that fail to see faults
errors.why: yan lag med pa is the Limbless One (Anaṅga/Kāma) or the missing faculty that would see faults; in neither reading is the body wasted 'by limbs'.

errors.english: Or will she stir herself and come at night
errors.why: The lover asks whether he himself should set out and go at night while people sleep; it is not the woman coming.

errors.english: the fire of the limbs arises
errors.why: This is most likely the fire of Anaṅga (yan lag med, the god of love), not a 'fire of the limbs'.

errors.english: They embrace women who are like a blazing fire born of iron and pervaded by sparks.
errors.why: This is the hell punishment, in which adulterers embrace a woman of blazing iron covered with sparks; it is not a simile for women in this life.

errors.english: Moving with elegance, her two breasts are high and auspicious.
errors.why: The bodhisattva's discourse is in long-metre verse (four-line stanzas closing with a śloka), and all of it is rendered as running prose.

note: The bodhisattva's verses against desire are given in prose, and several lines mistake who acts and where (hell versus this life). A specialist needs to revise the verse.

errors.english: is also the (Pradhana) Fundamental Nature/Primary Matter; however, this is said to be utterly hollow and lacking inherent nature
errors.why: The Sāṃkhya verse says that whatever comes into view is utterly hollow and without essence; it does not assert that the visible is the Pradhāna, and nothing in the text corresponds to 'however'.

note: The reductio against the Sāṃkhya pradhāna (if the manifest effects are hollow, so is their cause) is followed faithfully except in the cited verse.
